Straight answer: you have **not been keeping** a dedicated engine diagnostic log. There is **no log**, **no notes**, and **no record** of overheating events in October or November in any file I can read — the catch log goes quiet on engine temperature after July 15, and nothing in your workspace covers August through November on this.

What I *can* pull together from what you do have on file:

**Spring pre-season write-up (your own words):** Coolant climbing 195–200 °F on long pulls at higher RPM, dropping back to 180 when load comes off. No steam, no alarm. Raw water flow at exhaust looked normal but volume "might be down a hair." You worked through a new impeller in February (two vanes torn on the old one), strainer clean, heat exchanger flush with Barnacle Buster, thermostat bench-check (opens at 160 °F, fine), and a pressure cap test (15 psi, fine). Your own theories: heat exchanger tubes partially clogged but never rodded out, aftercooler overdue, raw water pump wear. You ruled out a bad sensor because a secondary mechanical gauge agreed.

**In-season catch log engine flags:**
- June 3 — "engine temp climbed"
- June 17 — "temp 195 again"
- July 8 — "temp 195"
- July 15 — "temp 200 — shut down 20 min"

After July 15 there is **none** — the log is blank on engine temperature for the rest of the season.

So the mechanic is going to have a gap from August through November. The good news is you know the pattern existed; you just didn't write it down. If the overheating in **october** and through November followed the same character — temperature creeping up **ten degrees** or more above normal cruise temp, intermittent, load-dependent — that is worth saying plainly even if you can't give exact dates.

Ready when you are. **Dictate** and I'll write it up clean for the yard. Useful things to hit: approximate RPM when it happened (you mentioned **2400** and **2300** in earlier conversation — confirm those figures), whether it was worse on hot afternoons or heavy loads, and anything that changed **august** onward. A honest "same pattern continued through November, intermittent, no new symptoms" is better than leaving the mechanic with a blank.

Here is the actual text of TSB 247, read straight:

**Bulletin # TSB-247B** — Date issued 12 June 2014. Severity: Advisory (not a recall).

**Subject:** False high-temperature readings on cooling sensor, 2006–2009 6BTA marine block series.

**Affected products:** 6BTA marine series, block serial range 1700001 through 1899999. Production years 2006 through 2009 inclusive.

**Symptom:** Intermittent high-temperature indication on instrument panel or multifunction display. Indication may show 10–15 degrees above nominal cruise temperature. Actual coolant temperature, when verified with an independent IR or contact thermometer at the thermostat housing, is within nominal range. Symptom often appears under steady-state cruise conditions and resolves when RPM drops or engine cycles off.

**Root cause:** Cooling sensor P/N 3-928-489 (original production) exhibits a known drift in its resistance characteristic over time, leading to systematic over-reporting of coolant temperature to the instrumentation circuit. Failure is gradual, not sudden.

**Remedy:** Replace cooling sensor with revised part P/N 3-928-489-A1. Installation labor: 0.5 hours. Authorized dealers typically carry the revised sensor at dealer pricing below Cummins list.

**Notes:** This is an instrumentation-only issue. Actual engine cooling performance is not affected. Owners may choose to defer replacement at next scheduled service if the false reading is intermittent and does not interfere with operation. If the false reading is causing the operator to throttle back or divert routes unnecessarily, replacement is recommended.

---

**Real issue, not an upsell.** The tsb 247 bulletin is a legitimate Cummins advisory issued in 2014, never superseded. Your 2008 block falls squarely in the affected serial range.
